title_original: Midjourney: Report Claims AI Model Is Worst Offender For Flouting Hollywood Copyright

blocks.text: EXCLUSIVE : Disney and NBCUniversal accused Midjourney of being a “bottomless pit of plagiarism” in a lawsuit last year . More than 18 months on, the company allegedly has failed to clean up its act.

VN. ai , a tech startup that stress tests generative artificial intelligence tools for copyright infringement, has produced its first quarterly report examining how 15 popular AI models performed when it comes to flouting studio IP.

blocks.text: The research conducted last month found that Midjourney v8.1 was the worst offender when it came to reproducing images of copyrighted characters. The AI model also outranked competitors on so-called “brand safety violations,” meaning characters were placed in a “harmful context,” such as scenes of violence or drug taking.

blocks.text: According to VN.ai’s report, which was shared with Deadline, Midjourney reproduced images of characters that violated brand safety measures once in every three text prompts, or 37% of the time. This included a Midjourney v8.1 hallucination in which it generated an image of The Joker smoking cannabis while wearing a dress that could have been ripped from the wardrobe of Frozen’s Elsa.

Midjourney did not respond to requests for comment. Disney and NBCUniversal’s lawsuit against the company remains ongoing, and Warner Bros Discovery also has filed suit . The startup has argued that training its AI models on images of copyrighted material is permitted under fair use.

links.text: Warner Bros Discovery also has filed suit

blocks.text: VN.ai’s report found that every AI model generated at least one copyright-protected character, even when a character’s name was not referenced in a text prompt. This included Google’s Nano Banana and ByteDance’s model Seedance 2.5, though the latter has improved significantly after receiving cease-and-desist letters from Hollywood studios.

As noted recently by Deadline, other Chinese AI models continue to plunder IP , including MiniMax H3, which generated videos that violated studio brand safety standards 55% of the time when an image was used in a prompt.

links.text: Chinese AI models continue to plunder IP

blocks.text: Asked why AI models continue to flout copyright, VN.ai founder Nelson Chu said it was “good for business.” He added: “It’s great marketing. It works. It gets people to use your model and pay for it.”

Chu predicts change, however. “I do think at some point that’s just not going to be OK. And I think as more models set the precedent for how it is to be a good actor here, you will see more improvement,” he told Deadline.
